mcqs.question: Why is a schema change on an event bus riskier than a change behind a single synchronous API?
options: Event buses don't support versioning at all
APIs never have multiple clients, so there's nothing to coordinate
The producer can't know which consumers are listening or when they'll next deploy, so old and new schema readers can coexist for a long time
Event buses always require a full system outage to change a schema
mcqs.explanation: The producer's lack of visibility into who's consuming and when they'll deploy is exactly why old and new schemas coexist longer than they would behind an API you control both sides of. Event buses do support versioning, APIs can have many clients too, and schema changes don't require an outage.

mcqs.question: A team adds a new optional field with a default value to an event schema. Which compatibility direction does this preserve?
options: Neither — any schema change breaks both directions
Only forward compatibility, not backward
Only backward compatibility, not forward
Both — old consumers ignore the unrecognized field, and new consumers get the default when reading an old message
mcqs.explanation: An optional field with a default is the textbook safe change: it satisfies both directions at once, since old readers simply skip it and new readers fill in the default for older messages. It's not true that any change breaks both directions, and this specific change doesn't favor only one direction.

mcqs.question: What does a schema registry do that a topic owner writing a compatibility policy in a wiki page doesn't?
options: Mechanically rejects an incompatible schema at publish time, rather than relying on every engineer to remember and follow the policy
Automatically rewrites old messages to match any new schema
Eliminates the need for consumers to handle any schema differences at all
Guarantees every consumer redeploys immediately after a schema change
mcqs.explanation: The registry's value is enforcement at the moment of publish, not documentation of a rule engineers might forget. It doesn't rewrite historical messages, doesn't remove the need for sensible schema design in consumers, and can't force anyone to redeploy.

mcqs.question: Which of these is a breaking change for a consumer reading events by field name?
options: Adding a new optional field with a default
Renaming an existing field, like customerId to userId
Adding an entirely new event type
Adding a new optional field with no default, on a topic where consumers already ignore unrecognized fields
mcqs.explanation: A rename makes the old field name vanish for anyone reading by name, which is breaking even though the underlying data still exists under a new name. The other three options are all safe additions that don't remove or change anything existing consumers already rely on.

mcqs.question: A producer renames customerId to userId in one deploy, with no transition period. What's the likely outcome across five downstream consumer services on different deploy schedules?
options: Nothing — renaming a field never affects consumers
All five consumers fail loudly and immediately at the same moment
Each consumer independently breaks or silently mishandles the missing field whenever it next processes the new schema, discovered on different days
The event bus automatically maps the old field name to the new one for every consumer
mcqs.explanation: Because each service deploys and processes messages on its own schedule, the failure surfaces at different times for each one rather than all at once, which is what makes this class of bug hard to trace back to a single cause. Brokers don't auto-map renamed fields, and the rename does affect anything reading the old field name.
